Build
bild
v.t. (rendering Hebrew banah, Greek oikodomeō)
From Saxon byldan, to construct a dwelling, from bold, a house. Hebrew banah means to build, and the noun bēn, a son, comes from the same root — a man builds his house by his children, which is why Scripture says a barren woman is built up when the LORD gives her a son.

Biblical Definition

Building in Scripture is never merely construction; it is the making of something meant to last, and the first question is always whose work it is. The Psalm states the governing principle in one line: “Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it” (Psalm 127:1) — not a discouragement of labour but a denial that labour is sufficient. The Lord Jesus claims the building of His own house and guarantees the outcome: “upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18) — the church is His project, and its permanence is His promise, not the builders'. Paul, having laid a foundation, warns every man who works on it: “let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon” (1 Corinthians 3:10), and the fire of the day of judgment will test the material. And Nehemiah gives the human side of the work its finest sentence: “So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work” (Nehemiah 4:6). Set together these four texts form the whole doctrine of Christian labour: God builds or nothing stands; Christ builds His church infallibly; men build on His foundation answerably; and the people who actually get walls finished are the people with a mind to work.

Webster 1828 Definition

To construct, erect, or raise, as an edifice; to establish and increase. In Scripture, the vanity of building without the LORD, Christ's promise to build His church against which hell shall not prevail, the warning to take heed how a man builds on the foundation, and the wall built by a people with a mind to work.

expand to see more

BUILD, v.t. 1. To frame, construct and raise, as an edifice or fabric of almost any kind.

2. To raise by art; to frame or shape into a particular form; as, to build a ship.

3. To increase and strengthen; to cement or unite; to establish; as, to build up a family or a church.

4. From Saxon byldan, to build, from bold, a dwelling; Hebrew banah, to build.

5. In Scripture, except the LORD build the house, Ps. 127; upon this rock I will build my church, Matt. 16.

Key Scripture

Psalm 127:1 — "A Song of degrees for Solomon. Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain."

Matthew 16:18 — "And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it."

1 Corinthians 3:10 — "According to the grace of God which is given unto me, as a wise masterbuilder, I have laid the foundation, and another buildeth thereon. But let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon."

Nehemiah 4:6 — "So built we the wall; and all the wall was joined together unto the half thereof: for the people had a mind to work."

Modern Corruption

Church growth is treated as a construction problem to be solved by method, so that what men build is credited to God; and Matthew 16:18 is bent into a claim for one bishop's successors rather than a promise about Christ's own work.

expand to see more

Rome reads Matthew 16:18 as the charter of the papacy: Peter is the rock, the office is perpetual, and the bishop of Rome inherits it. The text will not carry the weight. The Lord addresses Peter by the name He had given him and then shifts the word — thou art Petros, and upon this petra I will build — and the New Testament everywhere identifies the foundation otherwise: other foundation can no man lay than that is laid, which is Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 3:11), and the household of God is built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Jesus Christ Himself being the chief corner stone (Ephesians 2:20). Peter himself, writing later, calls Christ the living stone and every believer a stone in the building, and never hints at a successor. The confession Peter had just made — Thou art the Christ, the Son of the living God — is what the church is built on, and it is the promise, not the office, that hell cannot prevail against.

The practical corruption is nearer to most churches than the papal one. Where growth is treated as a technique — the right programme, the right music, the right demographic study — a congregation may be built rapidly and be built of wood, hay, and stubble. Paul does not forbid care in building; he commands it, telling every man to take heed how he builds, which assumes real responsibility and real skill. What he denies is that the work will escape testing. The fire shall try every man's work of what sort it is, and a man may be saved yet suffer loss with a lifetime's building burnt at his feet. The principle to recover joins Psalm 127 to Nehemiah 4: labour without God is vain, and God's building nevertheless goes up through people who have a mind to work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew banah, to build, and by figure to establish a family; binyan, a building; Greek oikodomeō, to build a house, whence oikodomē, edification.

expand to see more

Hebrew banah (H1129) — to build, rebuild, establish; also used of God building Eve from Adam's rib (Genesis 2:22).

Hebrew bēn (H1121) — a son; from the same root as banah, since sons are how a house is built.

Greek oikodomeō (G3618) — to build a house; used of Christ building His church and of believers edifying one another.

Greek oikodomē (G3619) — a building, and figuratively edification; “ye are God's building” (1 Corinthians 3:9).

Greek themelios (G2310) — a foundation; the foundation laid by the wise masterbuilder (1 Corinthians 3:10-11).

Usage

"Of the insufficiency of labour alone: Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it (Psalm 127:1)."

"Of Christ's indestructible work: upon this rock I will build my church (Matthew 16:18)."

"Of accountable workmanship: let every man take heed how he buildeth thereupon (1 Corinthians 3:10)."
